rationale: USP <797> specifies sampling **≥ 1 cubic meter (1000 L)** of air per location so the result is statistically meaningful. Action levels are then >1 (ISO 5), >10 (ISO 7), and >100 cfu/m³ (ISO 8).

stem: USP General Chapter **<71>** describes:

opts.A: Viable air sampling of the cleanroom
opts.B: The sterility test performed on the compounded **product** (not air)

rationale: **USP <71> is *Sterility Tests*** — it tests the **CSP/product** for sterility. Air is monitored by volumetric impaction under <797>/<1116>; <71> does not test air.

stem: The two methods of sterility testing described in USP <71> are:

opts.B: Membrane filtration (preferred) and direct inoculation (direct transfer)

rationale: USP <71> uses **membrane filtration** (the preferred method) and **direct inoculation / direct transfer**. Impaction/settling are air methods; gravimetric/volumetric are ACD accuracy; steam/dry heat are sterilization.

stem: The incubation period for a USP <71> sterility test is:
rationale: USP <71> sterility tests are incubated for **14 days** before a result is read, allowing slow-growing organisms to appear.

stem: USP <71> sterility testing uses which media/temperatures?

opts.B: Fluid thioglycollate medium (30–35°C) and soybean–casein digest medium (20–25°C)

rationale: USP <71> uses **fluid thioglycollate medium (FTM) at 30–35°C** (recovers aerobes and anaerobes) and **soybean–casein digest medium (SCDM/TSB) at 20–25°C** (recovers aerobes and fungi).

stem: A Category 2 CSP compounded from **one or more nonsterile components** is most commonly rendered sterile by:

opts.B: Sterilization by filtration through a 0.22 µm membrane (aseptic processing), or terminal sterilization

rationale: Nonsterile starting components must be **sterilized** — typically **0.22 µm sterilizing filtration** (aseptic processing) or terminal sterilization. Note filtration is **not** terminal sterilization, because it is not a lethal process.

stem: An **injectable** Category 2 CSP made from nonsterile components that is assigned a **sterility-tested** BUD also requires:
rationale: Injectable CSPs made from nonsterile components carry endotoxin risk, so a **bacterial endotoxin test** is required when a sterility-tested BUD is used (and always for Category 3 injectables from nonsterile components).

stem: Are **ophthalmic** CSPs required to undergo **bacterial endotoxin** testing?

opts.B: No — ophthalmic preparations are not Category 2 injectables, so endotoxin testing is not required (though they must still be sterile)
opts.D: Only if made from sterile components

rationale: Ophthalmics are applied to the eye, not injected into the bloodstream, so **endotoxin testing is not required**. They must still be **sterile** and are subject to sterility testing when applicable.

stem: Which testing requirement applies to an **ophthalmic** CSP?

opts.B: Sterility (it must be sterile; sterility-tested when applicable), but endotoxin testing is not required

rationale: Ophthalmic CSPs **must be sterile** (and undergo sterility testing when applicable), but **endotoxin testing is not required** because they are not injectable Category 2 preparations.

stem: Does USP <797> apply to CSPs compounded for **veterinary (animal) patients**?

opts.B: Yes — <797> covers CSPs for both human and animal patients
opts.D: Only if the same drug is used in humans

rationale: USP <797> applies to sterile compounding for **both human and animal patients**. Veterinary status does not exempt a preparation from the chapter’s standards.

stem: For a CSP prepared for a **non-human (veterinary)** patient, the **bacterial endotoxin limit** is calculated:

opts.A: The same fixed limit used for humans
opts.B: Per USP <85>, using the dose and body weight of the **target animal species**
opts.C: It does not apply to animals
opts.D: Based only on the drug’s concentration

rationale: Endotoxin limits are **species- and weight-specific**: for a non-human patient they are calculated per **USP <85>** using the intended dose and the **body weight of the target species**, since a small animal tolerates far less endotoxin than a human.

stem: **Terminal sterilization** is best defined as:

opts.A: Removing microorganisms by passing a solution through a filter
opts.B: Sterilizing the product in its **final sealed container** using a lethal process (e.g., steam, dry heat, irradiation, or gas)
opts.C: Disinfecting the outside of the container

rationale: **Terminal sterilization applies a lethal process to the product in its final sealed container** — steam, dry heat, irradiation, or gas. Filtration removes microbes but is not lethal, so it is aseptic processing, not terminal sterilization.

stem: Which of the following is **NOT** a terminal sterilization method?

opts.C: Sterilizing filtration through a 0.22 µm membrane

rationale: **Sterilizing filtration is not terminal sterilization** — it is not a lethal process and is done before final packaging. Steam, dry heat, and gas (and irradiation) are terminal (lethal) methods.

stem: Why is **sterilizing filtration** not considered terminal sterilization?

opts.B: It removes microorganisms but is not a lethal process applied to the product in its final container
opts.C: It can only be used on powders

rationale: Filtration **physically removes** organisms rather than killing them, and it is performed before final packaging — so it does not meet the definition of a **lethal, final-container** (terminal) process.

stem: Which terminal method is used to sterilize **heat- and moisture-stable** equipment and instruments?
rationale: **Steam autoclaving** is the method of choice for heat- and moisture-stable equipment/instruments — efficient and non-toxic. Dry heat is for anhydrous items; gas is reserved for heat-sensitive devices.

stem: Which method is used to sterilize **heat-stable but moisture-sensitive** items such as oils, powders, glassware, and metal?
rationale: **Dry heat** sterilizes anhydrous/moisture-sensitive materials that steam cannot penetrate — oils, powders, glassware, and metal — using higher temperatures for longer times.

stem: Which method is appropriate for sterilizing **heat-sensitive** equipment or devices that cannot be autoclaved?

opts.C: Ethylene oxide gas (or a low-temperature method such as vaporized hydrogen peroxide)

rationale: Heat-sensitive devices use a **low-temperature method — ethylene oxide gas or vaporized hydrogen peroxide**. Steam and dry heat would damage them; depyrogenation is a high-heat endotoxin process.

stem: The most common terminal sterilization method for heat- and moisture-stable **aqueous CSPs** is:
rationale: **Steam autoclaving** is the most common terminal method for aqueous products and equipment that tolerate heat and moisture — typically 121°C, 15 psi, for 15–60 minutes.

stem: All of the following are **terminal (lethal)** sterilization methods EXCEPT:
rationale: **Sterilizing filtration is the exception** — it removes rather than kills organisms and is not a terminal process. Steam, dry heat, and irradiation are all terminal lethal methods.

stem: Is **5-fluorouracil (5-FU)** a hazardous drug?

opts.A: No — it is exempt because it is a pyrimidine
opts.B: Yes — it is an antineoplastic (NIOSH Group 1) hazardous drug

rationale: **5-FU is an antineoplastic hazardous drug (NIOSH Group 1)** and must be handled under USP <800> containment and PPE requirements.

stem: Which of the following is a **hazardous drug** under USP <800>?
rationale: **Cisplatin is an antineoplastic hazardous drug (NIOSH Group 1).** Saline, dextrose, and sterile water are not hazardous drugs.

stem: Is **ganciclovir** a hazardous drug?

opts.B: Yes — it is NIOSH-listed (Group 2, non-antineoplastic) for carcinogenic/teratogenic/genotoxic risk

rationale: **Ganciclovir is a hazardous drug — NIOSH Group 2 (non-antineoplastic).** Although it is an antiviral, it is listed because of carcinogenic, teratogenic, and genotoxic properties.

stem: **Mitomycin** and **cisplatin** are classified as:

opts.D: Hazardous waste but not hazardous drugs

rationale: **Mitomycin and cisplatin are antineoplastic hazardous drugs (NIOSH Group 1)** — requiring full <800> containment, PPE, and (when the dosage form allows) a CSTD.

stem: NIOSH **Group 1** hazardous drugs are:

opts.C: Drugs that are only environmental hazards

rationale: **NIOSH Group 1 = antineoplastic drugs** such as 5-FU, cisplatin, mitomycin, and cyclophosphamide. Group 2 is non-antineoplastic hazardous drugs; Group 3 is drugs with primarily reproductive/developmental risk.

stem: A drug meets the USP <800>/NIOSH definition of a **hazardous drug** if it:

opts.B: Appears on the NIOSH list or meets NIOSH hazard criteria (carcinogenicity, teratogenicity, reproductive or developmental toxicity, organ toxicity at low doses, genotoxicity, or similarity to an existing HD)

rationale: An HD is any drug **on the NIOSH list or meeting the NIOSH hazard criteria** — carcinogenicity, teratogenicity/developmental toxicity, reproductive toxicity, organ toxicity at low doses, genotoxicity, or structure/toxicity resembling an existing HD.

stem: Appropriate PPE for **compounding** an antineoplastic hazardous drug includes:

opts.A: A single pair of latex exam gloves
opts.B: Two pairs of ASTM D6978–tested chemotherapy gloves and a disposable, low-permeability chemotherapy gown
opts.C: No gown if a C-PEC is used

rationale: HD compounding requires **double chemotherapy gloves (ASTM D6978) and a disposable, back-closing, low-permeability chemotherapy gown**, plus head/hair/shoe covers and appropriate eye/respiratory protection as indicated.

stem: Under USP <800>, a **closed-system drug-transfer device (CSTD)**:

opts.B: Must be used when **administering** antineoplastic HDs (when the dosage form allows) and should be used when **compounding** them
opts.C: Replaces the need for a C-PEC

rationale: A **CSTD must be used for administration** of antineoplastic HDs when the dosage form allows, and **should be used for compounding** them. It supplements — does not replace — the C-PEC/containment.

stem: USP <800> **medical surveillance** of personnel who handle hazardous drugs refers to:

opts.B: A program of baseline and periodic health assessment to detect early signs/effects of HD exposure
opts.C: Checking their gloved fingertips for microbes

rationale: **Medical surveillance** is a health-focused program — baseline and periodic assessment (history, exam, and relevant tests) to detect **early effects of HD exposure** — distinct from competency testing or microbial sampling.

stem: How often must personnel who handle hazardous drugs have their **handling competency** reassessed under USP <800>?
rationale: USP <800> requires HD-handling **competency to be reassessed at least every 12 months** (and whenever a process or device changes).

stem: **Environmental wipe sampling** in an HD area is used to:

opts.B: Detect hazardous-drug surface contamination (performed initially as a benchmark and then routinely, e.g., every 6 months)

rationale: **Wipe sampling detects HD surface residue.** USP <800> recommends an initial benchmark and routine sampling (commonly ~every 6 months) to confirm containment and decontamination are effective.

stem: All of the following are hazardous drugs EXCEPT:
rationale: **0.9% sodium chloride is not a hazardous drug** — the exception. 5-FU, cisplatin, and mitomycin are all antineoplastic HDs.

stem: A **C-PEC** (containment primary engineering control) is:

opts.A: The room that houses the compounding cabinet
opts.B: The device in which hazardous drugs are compounded (e.g., a Class II BSC or a CACI)

rationale: The **C-PEC is the primary containment device** where HDs are compounded — for sterile HD, a **Class II BSC or a CACI**. The room housing it is the C-SEC; a CSTD is a transfer device, not an engineering control.

stem: A **C-SEC** (containment secondary engineering control) for sterile HD compounding must be:

opts.B: Negative pressure (0.01–0.03″ WC), ≥30 ACPH, ISO 7, and externally vented
opts.C: Any ISO 8 room with positive pressure
opts.D: A room with no pressure requirement

rationale: The **C-SEC** (the room housing the C-PEC) must be **negative pressure 0.01–0.03″ WC**, provide **≥30 ACPH**, meet **ISO 7**, and be **externally vented** — containing HD contamination rather than protecting the CSP with positive pressure.

stem: The pressure differential of a hazardous-drug buffer room relative to adjacent areas is:
rationale: HD rooms are **negative 0.01–0.03″ WC** to contain hazardous drug aerosols/vapors — the opposite of the **positive** pressure used for non-HD sterile compounding.

stem: Which C-PEC is appropriate for **sterile** hazardous-drug compounding?

opts.B: A Class II biological safety cabinet (BSC) or a compounding aseptic containment isolator (CACI)
opts.D: An open bench in an ISO 7 room

rationale: Sterile HD compounding requires a **Class II BSC or a CACI** — both provide containment. A horizontal LAFW or a non-containment CAI blows air toward the worker and is prohibited for HDs.

stem: A C-PEC used for **antineoplastic** hazardous drugs must be:

opts.B: Externally vented (100% exhaust to the outside)

rationale: C-PECs for antineoplastic (and volatile) HDs must be **externally vented** — exhausted to the outside, not recirculated — and run **continuously** to maintain containment.

stem: The minimum total air changes per hour (ACPH) for an ISO 7 hazardous-drug buffer room is:
rationale: An ISO 7 HD buffer room requires **≥30 ACPH**, the same minimum as a non-HD ISO 7 buffer room — the difference for HD is the **negative** pressure and external venting.

stem: Why is a hazardous-drug compounding room kept at **negative** pressure, unlike a non-HD sterile room?

opts.A: To protect the CSP from the worker
opts.B: To contain hazardous-drug aerosols and vapors so they do not escape to adjacent areas

rationale: Negative pressure **contains HD contamination** within the room, protecting personnel and the environment. Non-HD sterile rooms are **positive** to protect the preparation from outside air — opposite goals.

stem: All of the following are required for a sterile-HD C-SEC EXCEPT:

opts.D: Positive pressure relative to adjacent areas

rationale: **Positive pressure is the exception** — an HD room must be **negative**. Negative pressure, ≥30 ACPH, and external venting are all required.

stem: For **nonsterile** hazardous-drug compounding, the appropriate C-PEC is:

opts.B: A containment ventilated enclosure (CVE) or a Class I BSC (an externally vented containment device)
opts.D: No containment is needed for nonsterile HDs

rationale: Nonsterile HD compounding uses a **containment ventilated enclosure (CVE) or a Class I BSC** — an externally vented containment device (a Class II BSC may also be used). Nonsterile HDs still require containment.

stem: How many mL of a **50% stock** solution are needed to prepare **100 mL of a 10%** solution?
You need **250 mL of 0.45% NaCl** starting from **0.9% NaCl** (diluted with sterile water). How much 0.9% NaCl is required?
rationale: (0.9%)(V1) = (0.45%)(250 mL) → V1 = 112.5/0.9 = **125 mL** of 0.9% NaCl, then add sterile water to make 250 mL.

stem: How many mL of **23.4% NaCl** are needed to make **1000 mL of 0.9% NaCl**?
How many mL of **D50W** are needed to prepare **500 mL of D10W**?
To prepare **75 mL of D12.5%** using **D70W** and **D5W**, how much **D70W** is needed?
For that same **75 mL of D12.5%** from D70W and D5W, how much **D5W** is needed?
rationale: D5 = (57.5/65)(75) = **66.35 mL**. Together with 8.65 mL of D70W this totals 75 mL at 12.5%.

stem: To make **1000 mL of D20W** from **D70W** and **D5W**, how much **D70W** is required?
In alligation with a high and a low concentration, the **parts of the higher** concentration equal:

opts.A: The higher concentration minus the lower
opts.B: The desired concentration minus the lower concentration
opts.C: The higher concentration minus the desired

rationale: Parts of the **higher** source = **desired − lower**; parts of the **lower** source = **higher − desired**. (The difference taken across the alligation diagonal.)

stem: A **1:1000** solution contains how many mg/mL?
rationale: 1:1000 = 1 g per 1000 mL = 1000 mg / 1000 mL = **1 mg/mL**. (Epinephrine 1:1000 = 1 mg/mL.)

stem: A **1:10,000** solution contains how many mg/mL?
How many **grams of dextrose** are in **75 mL of D12.5%**?
**2% lidocaine** contains how many mg/mL?
rationale: 2% = 2 g/100 mL = 2000 mg/100 mL = **20 mg/mL**. (Percent × 10 = mg/mL for w/v solutions.)

stem: What is the pressure differential between a **negative-pressure HD buffer room** and its adjacent **ante room**?

opts.B: Negative 0.01 to 0.03″ WC (the buffer is negative relative to the ante room)

rationale: The HD buffer room is **negative 0.01–0.03″ WC relative to the ante room**, so air flows from the ante room into the buffer, containing hazardous drugs.

stem: The **ante room** leading into a negative-pressure HD buffer room should be:

opts.A: Negative pressure to all adjacent areas
opts.B: Positive pressure (≥ 0.02″ WC) relative to adjacent unclassified areas, and ISO 7

rationale: The ante room is **positive (≥ 0.02″ WC) to the unclassified areas** and maintained at **ISO 7**. It is positive to the outside but higher than the negative HD buffer — so air moves ante → HD buffer.

stem: In a sterile HD suite, the airflow/pressure cascade is:

opts.A: From the HD buffer out to the ante room
opts.B: From the ante room into the negative-pressure HD buffer (higher → lower pressure)
opts.D: From outside directly into the HD buffer

rationale: Air cascades from **higher to lower pressure: ante room (positive) → HD buffer (negative)**. This directional flow keeps hazardous-drug contamination contained within the buffer room.

stem: A **non-hazardous positive-pressure buffer room** is measured at **+0.010″ WC** relative to the ante room. This reading is:

opts.B: Below the required minimum of +0.020″ WC — out of range (fails)
opts.C: Too high — it exceeds the maximum

rationale: A non-HD positive buffer requires a **minimum of +0.020″ WC** — a floor, not a range. **+0.010″ WC is only half the minimum, so it fails.** (The 0.01–0.03″ range belongs to the HD negative buffer, which is why 0.01 can feel “in range” but is not, here.)

stem: A measured differential of **0.01″ WC** is within the acceptable range for which room?

opts.B: A hazardous-drug negative-pressure buffer room (range 0.01–0.03″ WC)

rationale: **0.01″ WC is the low end of the HD negative buffer range (0.01–0.03″ WC)** — acceptable there. For a **non-HD positive** buffer the requirement is **≥ +0.020″ WC**, so 0.01 is below minimum and not acceptable.

stem: Which correctly pairs the room with its pressure specification?

opts.A: Non-HD positive buffer = 0.01–0.03″ WC; HD negative buffer = +0.020″ WC
opts.B: Non-HD positive buffer = ≥ +0.020″ WC (minimum); HD negative buffer = 0.01–0.03″ WC (range)
opts.C: Both use a minimum of +0.020″ WC

rationale: The **non-HD positive buffer has a minimum of +0.020″ WC**; the **HD negative buffer uses the 0.01–0.03″ WC range**. Swapping these two specs is the classic error.

stem: Why can **0.01″ WC** be acceptable in one compounding room but not another?

opts.B: Because the HD negative buffer allows 0.01–0.03″ WC (0.01 = low end), while the non-HD positive buffer requires a ≥ +0.020″ WC minimum
opts.D: Because only Category 3 rooms have requirements

rationale: The value is judged against **different specs**: the HD negative buffer’s **range (0.01–0.03)** includes 0.01, but the non-HD positive buffer’s **minimum (0.020)** does not. Same number, two different standards.

stem: A suite is tested for particle count **during compounding** and again **after the suite was empty**. Which measurement determines the room’s **ISO classification**?

opts.B: The count taken during compounding (dynamic/operational conditions)

rationale: ISO classification is determined under **dynamic (operational) conditions — during actual compounding with personnel present.** The empty/static count does not establish the class, because the room must stay within limits while it is in use.

stem: **Dynamic (operational)** testing conditions mean the room is:

opts.A: Complete but with no personnel or activity
opts.B: In operation with personnel present and performing normal compounding activities

rationale: **Dynamic/operational = the room in use — personnel present, equipment running, normal activity.** This represents the real (worst-case) particle load during compounding.

stem: **Static (at-rest)** conditions mean the room is:

opts.B: Complete with equipment operating but no personnel present and no activity
opts.C: Being certified for the first time

rationale: **Static/at-rest = equipment on but no people and no activity.** It is useful as a baseline but does not determine the ISO classification.

stem: How is a room’s ISO class determined from the particle count?

opts.A: The ≥0.5 µm particle count per m³ must stay at or below the ISO limit under dynamic conditions
opts.B: Any single reading below the limit at any time

rationale: The room is classified by whether the **≥0.5 µm particle count per cubic meter stays at/below the ISO limit while operating dynamically** (ISO 5 ≤3,520; ISO 7 ≤352,000; ISO 8 ≤3,520,000).

stem: Why is **dynamic** (in-use) particle testing required rather than empty-room testing alone?

opts.B: Because the room must meet its ISO limits during actual compounding — the real, worst-case condition when CSPs are exposed

rationale: Particles spike when **people and activity are present**, so the meaningful test is whether the room holds its ISO class **during compounding**. A room that passes empty but fails dynamically is not actually controlled when it matters.

stem: Under ISO 14644 / USP <797>, the ISO classification of a compounding room is certified in which occupancy state?
rationale: USP <797> certifies the ISO class in the **operational (dynamic)** state. ISO 14644 defines as-built, at-rest, and operational states; compounding certification uses the operational one.

stem: How often must the certified areas undergo recertification (including dynamic particle counts and airflow testing)?

opts.B: At least every 6 months (and after any change or servicing that could affect airflow)

rationale: Certification — including **dynamic particle counts, airflow/smoke studies, pressure, and ACPH** — must be repeated **at least every 6 months**, and whenever a change could affect airflow (e.g., moving the PEC, HEPA service).
